If you are looking to streamline your cable management and need reliable, fast charging for multiple demanding devices at once, this is absolutely worth the investment. It is incredibly well built, intelligent in how it safely distributes power, and highly efficient.

To expand on why this device operates so effectively and to provide thorough technical context, the use of Gallium Nitride (GaN) is the key differentiator here. Traditional chargers use silicon transistors, which have limits on thermal and electrical efficiency. GaN is a crystal-like semiconductor material that conducts electrons far more efficiently than silicon. This allows the internal components to be placed much closer together without the risk of overheating. The result is a charging block that is physically smaller, generates significantly less waste heat, and converts AC power from your wall into DC power for your devices much faster.

Additionally, a charging station of this magnitude relies on intelligent power allocation microchips. When you plug in a device, the device and the charger perform a digital handshake. The smart chip reads the maximum safe wattage requested by the device's battery controller. It then actively recalculates and redistributes the total 800 watts across the active ports. This guarantees that a power-hungry laptop receives the high wattage it needs, while a smaller accessory like a smartwatch receives a safe, low-wattage trickle charge, protecting the longevity of your batteries.

[{"reviewer_name": "John Caravaggio", "star_rating": 5.0, "review_title": "Do you have an external drive that has a short cable?", "review_description": "I have a LITE-ON USB 2.0 External CD/DVD Writer Model eUAU108, manufactured in 2013, with an attached cable that is slightly less than 4 inches long. This model was an improvement over prior models, in that it requires only a single USB 2.0 connection, whereas previous models employed a Y-cable to enable connecting to 2 USB ports simultaneously for additional power. I have always felt that this drive was marginally capable of running on the 500 mA specification for USB 2.0 ports. I think this is the main reason for the ultra short cable - to minimize the voltage drop.

The short cable worked OK when I was using the drive with a laptop, but attempting to use it with a computer attached to the back of my flat screen monitor is a major problem. The USB ports are about a foot above the desktop, making it necessary to support the drive in some manner. This has always been problematic. I tried using the only USB extension cable that I had, a cheap dollar store cable, and it did not work at all.

My next thought was that I should purchase a higher quality, and obviously more expensive, USB cable, but I still had reservations. Would a longer cable, even of a higher quality, work? Why did LITE-ON force a short cable onto the consumer? They could have provided a USB port instead of an attached cable. I then thought of using a powered hub, which could solve the voltage/power issue, but I still wondered if there might be other signal quality issues that a longer cable might cause. I believe I was starting to overthink the matter at this point!

I started looking at the market of powered hubs and discovered that there was quite a variety, from no-name cheapies to surprisingly expensive higher end units. It was easy to eliminate the no-name cheapies because there were brand names I was familiar with that were very affordable. Then I discovered that some of the hubs were rated at 10 Gbps! Gotta have that feature, right? Even though I don't have a single device faster than 5 Gbps, I justified this feature on the basis of future-proofing. I figured it would only be a matter of time before I had devices of that speed. Later on I discovered that all the USB ports on the computer attached to the back of my monitor are 10 Gbps capable – five are USB 3.2 Gen2 (10 Gbps) and one is USB4 (40 Gbps!) - additional justification for going with a 10 Gbps hub.

As I looked at the 10 Gbps offerings I quickly discovered that many, if not most of them, were from RSHTECH/Rosonway. They have quite a variety of well designed, useful devices. So many options that I found it helpful to generate a table of features to more easily compare them. I finally decided to go with the RSH-H7C4 for the following reasons:

• 10 Gbps on every port

• both USB-A and USB-C ports

• push button switch (vs. rocker type), with an indicator light, for each port

• all ports support USB Battery Charging 1.2 protocol (BC1.2), delivering a maximum of 1.5A at 5V (7.5W) per port [standard USB ports limit current to 0.5A (USB 2.0) or 0.9A (USB 3.2)]

• 36W (12V/3A) DC power adapter

• detachable 3.3 foot USB-C host cable (when I need to connect to a USB-A host I use a cheap adapter I purchased at a dollar store; some of the Rosonway units include a dual-headed cable with both A and C plugs!)

• two year warranty

It's a beautifully designed unit with a solid, weighty feel to it. Rounded edges and a thin accent band of non-anodized aluminum around each end give this hub a modern, classy appearance. With the case being narrow and slightly rounded on the bottom, one might have concern about its stability against the pushing and pulling of the connected USB cables. While it might technically be more stable with a completely flat bottom, it is surprisingly stable as is due to its weight and mass. Not at all like some of the lighter weight plastic cased devices that I have. It would take a deliberate effort to tip it over; I don't think that will be an issue. I actually do tip it over to accommodate one of my situations: the cable on my DVD drive is so short that the drive cannot lay flat when the cable is inserted into the port on the hub from above. I have to lay the hub on its side (see video).

The included USB cable is heavy gauge, very thick. With my limited experience in the world of USB cables I have made two observations: 1)there is a tremendous range of cost, quality, and capabilities among the many cables on the market; 2)an extra USB cable frequently comes in handy. It would make sense to me that RSHTECH would provide a suitably high-grade cable with their hub in order to support the 10 Gbps data rate and the BC1.2 current draw capability. The fact that the USB cable is detachable is a bonus! It can be used elsewhere. I could even change it into an extension cable by the use of a gender-changing adapter.

The indicator lights are a beautiful blue, quite small, but tastefull in my opinion; apparently too small for some reviewers, but I have no complaint. I would rather have them understated than overstated.

The first testing I did was to connect the aforementioned LITE-ON CD/DVD writer to the computer hanging on the back of my monitor using the RSH-H7C4 hub and its included USB cable. (When the LITE-ON drive is directly attached to this computer I never have problems because the power requirement of the LITE-ON drive is easily satisfied.) I briefly tried the hub in “bus-powered” mode (without the power supply attached). I was able to read files on the DVD writer with no problem. (This was just a brief, not comprehensive, test because my main concern was testing the more power intensive task of burning a disk.)

The next testing was in “self-powered” mode (with the power supply attached). I successfully burned and verified an ISO image. I then disconnected the power supply and tried to burn the image again in bus-powered mode. The burning went without any error messages, but the verification process failed. Another attempt in bus-powered mode failed during the burning process. Returning to self-powered mode (with the power supply attached), I was again able to successfully burn and verify the ISO image.

It appears that when the DVD writer is attached through the hub and cable, burning a disk requires additional power beyond what the computer port is supplying (in order to power the circuitry in the hub and to compensate for loss over the length of the three foot cable). USB Battery Charging 1.2 protocol (BC1.2) seems to do the job here. I am pleased with that! I have solved the short cable issue; I can now lay my DVD drive flat on the desk and have dependable operation.

Additional testing with a much older computer, a Dell Inspiron Mini 1012 (vintage 2010), revealed an unexpected limitation: the DVD writer was unable to be recognized as a boot device by the Inspiron Mini when connected to it through the hub. As far as I can tell, this is a limitation of the older BIOS in the Inspiron. There is no way to make this system recognize an optical drive connected via a USB hub at boot up. After the system is booted the drive is able to be used with no problem. It is my understanding that the more modern BIOSes of today handle this situation in a more sophisticated manner and can detect hub-connected optical drives at bootup. I verified this by bootup tests on the computer attached to my monitor and on a modern netbook. Both of those systems were able to recognize the DVD writer at bootup with no problem when it was connected via the hub.

The Dell Inspiron Mini 1012 has USB 2.0 ports that theoretically should supply enough power for the LITE-ON CD/DVD writer, but I have always felt that it was marginal. I would like to be able to supplement the power. The RSH-H7C4 is only a partial solution here. It can be used with the Inspiron for burning disks since that is a process that occurs after bootup, but in the case where I need to boot from this DVD writer I might have to first transfer the DVD image to a bootable USB thumb drive and use that instead.

While not a comprehensive evaluation of the RSH-H7C4, my tests have assured me that some of my problems have been solved. I can comfortably lay the LITE-ON CD/DVD writer on the desk instead of trying to figure out how to suspend it a foot up in the air in order to attach it to the computer hanging behind my flat screen monitor. I can also use the hub for more dependable disk burning using my Inspiron Mini 1012.

I am quite impressed with the RSH-H7C4 hub and RSHTECH/Rosonway. I've always been very excited by little “boxes” and devices that solve computer interconnection (and other) problems. The companies that come up with these solutions are frequently very clever. RSHTECH will now be one of the first companies I look to for such solutions. A brief look at their lineup shows devices such as:

• USB switches (to share USB ports between two computers)

• powered and unpowered USB hubs, some with card readers and HDMI ports

• powered USB extension cables

• unpowered USB extension cables with built-in signal booster chips

• USB HDD/SSD enclosures

• docking and cloning stations

• 10 Gbps USB connected M.2 NVME/SATA SSD enclosures

• 10 Gbps USB connected Magnetic M.2 NVME SSD enclosure with 100W PD

RSHTECH puts an effort into including enough hard facts and specifications in their product descriptions to enable consumers to easily understand a device’s capabilities and limitations. This fact, and my favorable impression of the RSH-H7C4 hub, give me confidence to expect good performance and value with any of their products.

Read more"}, {"reviewer_name": "william", "star_rating": 4.0, "review_title": "Solid powered USB hub that has performed in the time I have used it.", "review_description": "I have been in IT long enough to know that a USB hub is one of those products that sounds simple on paper but has a surprisingly wide range of quality in practice. I have also been burned enough times by bad ones to approach any new hub with a healthy dose of skepticism. So when I say that the Rosonway powered USB hub has genuinely impressed me, I want you to understand that it is coming from someone who does not hand out compliments to peripheral hardware easily.

I have had this hub for 13 days now. That might not sound like a long time, but in the context of my daily IT work, I have put it through what I would consider a serious run of testing. This is not a hub that has been sitting on a desk powering a wireless mouse dongle and a phone charger. It has been put through a ringer of a minimum of 12-14 hours 5-6 days a week. And it was used every day. With a rotating cast of demanding devices that would expose any weakness in a lesser product.

Why I Came Back to Rosonway

This is actually my second Rosonway hub. My first one is still running, still reliable, and was purchased specifically because I had grown so frustrated with other brands that I needed something I could actually count on. Before finding Rosonway the first time, I dealt with pretty much every problem a USB hub can throw at you — and often all at once. Devices dropping connection randomly. Transfer speeds that had no business being as slow as they were, even on a nominally high-speed hub. Units that died within weeks of purchase. Build quality that felt like it might give out at any moment.

When you work in IT, unreliable hardware is not just an annoyance — it is a productivity problem and, at times, a professional one. The last thing I need in the middle of a task is a hub that decides to drop a device or throttle my speeds without warning. After going through several different brands and experiencing those issues repeatedly, I finally landed on Rosonway. My first unit solved all of those problems and has kept solving them ever since.

So when I needed more ports, the decision to go back to Rosonway was not really a decision at all. It was the obvious move based on earned trust. Sure you could go with more notorious brands, but the bang for my buck on this brand has been optimal.

Daily Use in an IT Context

My use case is not casual. I run this hub daily as part of an IT work setup that includes both a PC and a Mac, and I switch between the two regularly. Cross-platform reliability is something I specifically look for and specifically test, because a hub that works beautifully on Windows but causes headaches on macOS is only solving half my problem.

This one works correctly on both. No configuration differences, no quirks on one platform that do not exist on the other. It simply works the same way on both machines, which is exactly what you want.

The range of peripherals I have connected through this hub over the past 13 days is wide. I have been running a wired USB-C to 3.5mm DAC for my Corsair headset with microphone — and I want to flag this one specifically, because audio devices are often where cheaper hubs start to show their weaknesses. A DAC demands consistent, clean power delivery. Any instability shows up immediately as audio dropout, static, or microphone signal issues. This hub has delivered clean, uninterrupted audio and microphone performance every single time.

Beyond that, I have put external hard drives, thumb drives, and an SSD dock through this hub. External drives and SSD docks are about the most demanding things you can connect to a USB hub from a power and bandwidth standpoint. Drives pulling sustained power while transferring data will expose any inadequacy in a hub's power management quickly. I have had no issues — transfers run at expected speeds, the SSD dock behaves as if it is connected directly to the machine, and nothing has dropped or stuttered.

I have connected all of these devices in various combinations, not just one at a time. Running multiple demanding peripherals simultaneously is where a lot of hubs start to fall apart, and this one has handled every configuration I have thrown at it without complaint.

No Drivers, No Nonsense

One of the things I appreciated immediately was the plug-and-play experience. There were no extra drivers to hunt down and install. On both the PC and the Mac, I connected the hub and everything worked. That is the experience it should always be, but it is not always the experience you get — especially when you are working across two different operating systems.

Anyone who has spent time troubleshooting driver issues for what should be a simple USB hub knows how much time that can waste. The fact that this product required none of that was noticed and appreciated from day one.

The Physical Setup

The cable length on this hub is one of the practical details that does not always get mentioned in reviews but genuinely matters in a real workspace. It is long enough to allow for flexible positioning without being so long that it becomes a cable management problem. I was able to position the hub where it actually needed to be on my desk rather than compromising based on where the cable could reach. Small thing, but it adds up.

The hub is powered, which is worth emphasizing for anyone who has tried to run demanding devices off a bus-powered hub and wondered why things were not working right. Having dedicated power through the included adapter means each port has what it needs to perform, even with multiple devices pulling from it simultaneously. For the kind of peripherals I am running — drives, an SSD dock, a DAC — powered is not optional. It is required. This hub delivers that without any hesitation.

Thirteen Days and Counting

I want to be honest about what 13 days of heavy daily use tells you and what it does not. It does not give you years of long-term reliability data. What it does give you is a solid read on whether a product is going to perform under real working conditions without hand-holding. I have not been gentle with this hub, in terms of use. I have been plugging and unplugging devices frequently, running demanding transfers, switching between operating systems, and connecting combinations of peripherals that test the power distribution. In all of that, I have not encountered a single failure, dropout, connection issue, or performance problem.

That tracks with my experience with my first Rosonway hub, which is still running well after a year and half. The consistency between the two units tells me something about how Rosonway approaches quality control. It is one thing for one product to perform well. It is another for two separate purchases, at different times, to both deliver the same reliable experience.

Who This Hub Is For

If you are running a setup with demanding peripherals — external drives, audio devices, docking solutions — and you need something that will perform reliably across PC and Mac without driver headaches or connection instability, this hub is worth serious consideration. If you have been through the frustrating cycle of buying cheaper hubs, dealing with the problems they inevitably bring, and then replacing them, I understand that cycle because I lived it for longer than I should have.

The Rosonway powered USB hub is not the flashiest product in the world. It does not need to be. It has been dependable so far. It does exactly what it is supposed to do, every time, without requiring you to babysit it or troubleshoot it or work around its limitations. In the world of peripheral hardware, that kind of consistency is a huge bonus in my line of work.

Two for two on Rosonway products. I will be back if I need more ports. I am satisfied with my purchase.

[{"reviewer_name": "Aaron", "star_rating": 5.0, "review_title": "Great 10gbps USB-C Hub, worked with Anker support through compat issues with PD4 iteration 1", "review_description": "Original Review (updates below):

-----

The moment I noticed this thing on Amazon, I bought it and it literally just arrived. Finally, 4K60 over just USB-C with other ports (including making up to 10Gbps available to them) for a reasonable price. Unfortunately, the first two things I've done with it were both disappointing. I'll cut to the chase, the power delivery pass through isn't working with one of their own chargers.

The first device I tried connecting this with is my Anker PD4 with one USB-C cable as the only thing plugged into it so I can test the truly up to 100W (-15 for its own power) claims. I've tried connecting it with Apple's 2m USB-C charge cable (100w capable) and an equivalent CableMatters cable that also supports 100W. When plugged directly into my laptop, both of these cables immediately start charging it and show up as 100W power sources. When this Anker hub is plugged in and either of them is connected to the power delivery port on the side of it, the laptop does not charge (laptop is a 16" Macbook Pro, I've tried multiple ports just for the heck of it).

My second complaint is that when absolutely nothing is plugged into it, it becomes fairly warm to the touch. Why, when it's doing nothing, is it hot? I'm clearly not running data or even power through it so I have low hopes for it under load.

The fact that it doesn't work in exactly the scenario they want it to most (a MacBook Pro with one of their own chargers) seems like a pretty big fail. I've got lots of USB-C things though so I thought I'd grab a couple and try those. Using an Apple 96W USB-C charger, the device does pass through power delivery properly. It shows up as providing 79W to the laptop (siphoning off 17W in this instance). I also have a 56W Aukey charger that splits power between a USB-A port and a USB-C port that can provide 45W of power delivery. When plugged into that charger it does appear to work as well and appears in macOS as a 30W power source.

Maybe the problem is the Anker PD4? But it works fine providing power to the laptop directly. Would love to hear from Anker about these two products working together and what I should actually expect. Having it be unreliable for power delivery isn't great, but power and heat aside (it is getting a little bit warmer now that it's providing power from the Apple power adapter, but still definitely holdable), the hardware looks and feels good and the cable feels durable. Worth also noting that there's a white LED ring on the side of it that appears to be always on when it's plugged in. Don't know why it needs an LED.

-----

Update, June 22, 2020:

I've done some more testing and Anker has reached out to me to investigate what might be the issue. I can say that the hub works as I would expect from a quick test with my iPad Pro 11" with the above functioning chargers. It was able to pass through power with the 96W Apple Charger on the other end to both the iPad port as well as a Magic Keyboard port. The ethernet adapter showed up in iOS settings and an external drive was functional. When connected via the Magic Keyboard, which is a power only connection, as expected it provided only power.

Still no power passthrough of any kind when connected to the PD4.

-----

Update July 1, 2020:

I've written back and forth with Anker and they've sent me a replacement hub. It also doesn't work with the PD4. I've tried multiple USB-C cables but they have also shipped a cable to test with it. For now I'm increasing the review from 2 to 3 stars because I am more and more suspicious about the PD4 and less about this hub. They claim that they have tested the setup I have separately without issue, and I've sent video showing the problems I've encountered, so the troubleshooting is ongoing.

Have had a chance to use Ethernet on it without issue. Still need to try to test out its throughput when trying to use a 10Gbps USB-C enclosure and a 4K60 monitor at the same time (+ ethernet).

More updates to come.

-----

Update July 10, 2020:

I've continued to talk with Anker support and they shipped me a replacement PD4. The one I had was labeled as "Iteration 1" on its barcode, the one I got back was labeled "Iteration 2". This of course no longer allows HDMI on the Anker hub because the first dongle is using DP-alt mode for its HDMI, but it seems like if DP-alt mode is even _available_, the Anker's USB controller for Ethernet is limiting itself to 2.0 speeds.

While I only verified USB link speeds on Macbooks (via System Information), I found this so strange, as it means I can use this as an all-in-one-hub with slow Ethernet, OR as a data-only hub with full gigabit ethernet speeds. Doing both at once means I need another dongle either connected before or after it.

All other ports work great. I wish it had one more USB-C port of any speed.

If this was confusing to read, it was even more confusing to figure out, and I now have so many dongles working around this behavior that I have since put this dongle away. I no longer trust Anker to provide all advertised features.

Unfortunately, that's about where the positive news ends and as far as usability goes I cannot recommend this device. I've listed below the problems I experienced within the first 24 hours of usage:

1) The switches outright just do not work for many devices. I tried several devices which seem to somehow just "ignore" the switch being turned off. I put ignore in quotes, because the device should not be built in a way that would allow any attached device to communicate with the host while it's off. For some devices, the switch does work correctly. However, for other devices, I can plug a USB cable into the hub and have it persistently connected to the host no matter how many times I toggle the switch on and off. This is a key indicator that the device was not designed in a secure way. When the toggle switch is off, power and connectivity should be completely disconnected to the port. The fact that I am able to bypass the toggle switch is an indicator that some sort of firmware workaround is being used. Bad news here.

2) Power delivery does not seem to work correctly on the hub. I'm using the power adapter that was delivered with the device which is plugged into a stable power source. Some devices which require power delivery (USB-PD) get stuck in an initializing state when drawing power from the hub. They get enough power to appear powered on, but the device never initializes and the host system can detect something was plugged in but cannot interface with the device. When I switch these devices to a different hub (or directly to the host), the issue is not present and the device works as expected.

3) Even devices that do connect, seem to have issues with performance and/or connectivity. When some devices are attached to the hub, the host operating system seems to hang while the device is connecting. I experience this on about 1/3 of my attempts with any mass storage device, and some devices fairly consistently. When I do get a device to connect to the host, my transfer speeds are considerably lower than if I had used a different hub or connected directly to the host.

All in all, I absolutely do not recommend this device. There are several clear indicators of poor and unsafe design when it comes to this hub, and I would not trust that it delivers power cleanly or that there's any consistent integrity on file transfers.

Again, all of these issues were experienced within the first 24 hours of usage. I tested over a dozen different devices with this hub, of varying types and manufacturer. If I had this many issues straight away, I can guarantee it's not an isolated incident. Even if my hub was "defective", there's no way it would have been defective in a way that would selectively allow some devices to connect while toggled off.

Let this be a warning to you!

The backlight will turn off just a few seconds after you stop typing, and doesn't turn on again until you press a key. Updated review: beware the USB dongles.

Logitech mouses and keyboards (e.g. "MX Mechanical", "MX Master 3s", "MX Anywhere 3") connect either via Bluetooth, or via a USB dongle. However, the USB dongles are not all the same. For example, the "MX mechanical" keyboard only connects to a "bolt" dongle; and the "MX Anywhere 3" mouse only connects to a "unifying" dongle. Unfortunately, there is no clear guide / summary for which devices go together. You just have to check each device before buying to see what dongle it uses. Devices in the same generation are *not* guaranteed to use the same type of dongle.

Here is my experience: I setup for myself a MX mechanical keyboard + MX Master 3s mouse and everything works fine. Both devices connect to a "bolt" dongle, so I have a "bolt" dongle on my laptop, and another "bolt" dongle on a desktop computer. I can switch between laptop and desktop with a press of a button. The keyboard/mouse itself is fine, the review can be seen above.

My wife saw my setup and wanted the same, but she didn't want the MX Master 3s mouse ("it is too big"), so I got her a this same "MX Mechanical" keyboard and a pink "MX Anywhere 3". As it turns out, the mouse does not come with a "bolt" dongle, it comes with a "unifying" dongle. So now I have one "bolt" dongle which connects only to the keyboard, and one "unifying" dongle which connects only to the mouse. Thus, to "fix" this situation, I either need to use Bluetooth for everything (which I was trying to avoid to begin with), or I need to purchase 1 extra bolt dongle and 1 extra unifying dongle, so that each computer has both a "unifying" and a "bolt" dongle. Let's hope I have enough USB ports, or I will also need a USB hub.

Even if you are aware that different dongles exist, you still need to be careful. If you buy a "MX Anywhere 3", you get a "unifying" dongle, but if you buy a "MX Anywhere 3 for business", then it has a "bolt" dongle. This is, by the way, how I ended up with a "unifying" dongle - while browsing the products, I opened up two tabs, one with a black MX Anywhere 3, and one with a pink MX Anywhere 3, except one of them was "for business" and the other was not.

You might think this mess would warrant giant disclaimers ("DOES NOT HAVE A BOLT CONNECTOR"), or some kind of guide for which devices go together, but nope. For extra hilarity, Amazon bundles a "MX mechanical mini" (bolt) with a "MX Anywhere 3" (unifying). The whole thing is confusing, misleading, and just terrible user/customer experience. If I could start over, I would just get something else.

The feel is great and the pressure is just right to prevent most accidental touches to adjacent keys from inserting extra letters. Nice and clicky, maybe not the best for noise if you're in an office with other people, but the feel is great and if you work in a private office like I do the noise won't matter much. I had thought the RGB colors would be distracting, especially for an office, but actually they are fairly subdued and actually seem to help with positioning (I am a fast hunt-and-peck 3 finger typist, so this actually matters a lot to me).

I have a much more expensive Razer mechanical gaming keyboard at home, and the main difference I see between them, other than cosmetic differences, is that the Razer keys seem like they have a hair trigger and require very little motion to produce keystrokes, while this keyboard is a bit stiffer and requires the keys to be depressed a little harder in order to produce a keystroke. reviews:
[{"reviewer_name": "Z.", "star_rating": 5.0, "review_title": "Fantastic keyboard!!! Can't stop buying different colors. LOVE!!!", "review_description": "TL/DR (Updated): I now have this model in pink, black, and in blue, as well as a Mercury K1 Pro in black, and a GravaStar Mercury V75 HE keyboard in Lavender. They're all fantastic keyboards that are terrific straight out of the box, with zero customization, although if you don't NEED an HE keyboard, the mechanical keyboards offer better typing feel and sound by far - it's just the nature of HE keyboards - although they keep improving, and GravaStar's offering exceeded my expectations.

Admittedly, GravaStar's "bio-mechanical" styling is not for everyone (I love it), but it's amazing how much you can change up the looks with a simple keycap swap (if desired) and get a totally different vibe. I collect keycap sets, so I've swapped the keycaps on all but the HE board at this point. Battery life is fantastic - it feels endless if you forgo full RGB, and just have keys light up as you type (40 hours default lighting, over 400 with no RGB). I tend to save the full RGB effect (which I love) for those (infrequent) times when I'm charging the battery.

--------

This is my second type of GravaStar keyboard. I love my GravaStar Mercury K1 Pro (kitted with KiiBoom Sweet Rebel MAO profile keycaps) SO much that I couldn't resist picking up the Sakura Pink Special Edition K1 to go with my "Pixel Meow" MAO profile keycap set. Yet again, I could NOT be more delighted - both with the keyboard itself, and with how it paired with my keycaps of choice. I've included a quick photo (excuse the bad lighting), but it looks SO much better in person! Then, I had to get one in the pale blue. And then, I got one in black, because I had a different set of "pastel goth" keycaps and wanted a black keyboard for them.

If the funky, "bio-mechanical" rear legs of the Pro model are too thematically strong for your tastes, or they clash aesthetically with preferred third party keycaps, the K1 offers a more adaptable appearance; how the case is perceived will be strongly influenced by how you accessorize it. With the "retro Kawaii" Pixel Meow keycaps, especially with that beautiful Sakura Pink color I chose, the K1 just looks a bit fancy, given the relentlessly bio-mechanical-styled bottom is hidden while the keyboard is actually in use. If you paired the keyboard with, say, "Pastel Goth" keycaps, the keyboard case would go back to looking edgy and enhance that vibe.

I love that GravaStar has a detail-oriented approach to their keyboards. Unlike the (wonderful) matte finish on my black K1 Pro, the Sakura Pink K1 has a glossy, silky look and feel. I own more than twenty aluminum keyboards, and none of them have a finish like this. It's amazing! Interestingly, the volume rocker switch is in the same finish, instead of a metallic color, and I love how it feels to the touch.

I was also impressed that GravaStar customized the dongle's plastic body, instead of using the typical, generic (cheaper) shape. My black K1 Pro has a black plastic dongle (with a style that matches the keyboard body - awesome for easy visual identification AND aesthetics), while my Sakura Pink K1 has an identical-looking dongle, except in white. I love that I can look at either dongle and instantly know which keyboard it goes to. Not just between the two keyboards, but out of my entire collection.

The stock GravaStar-Kailh switches sound and feel wonderful, and look great through the translucent stock keycaps. The lighting isn't uniform, due to the opaque switch housing, which may bother some people, but for others, fully transparent switch housings may have made the RGB overkill.

The typing sound/pitch did (unfortunately, to my tastes) get a little bit higher with the MAO keycaps I installed on the keyboard vs. the stock, double-walled polycarbonate set, but it's still an incredible-sounding keyboard, just different. In a direct comparison, my PBT MAO keycaps sound slightly disappointing compared to the stock keyboard. In actual, ongoing use, the keyboard simply sounds utterly delicious. The keyboard is so well-tuned that I don't think you could make it sound bad unless you really tried.

I did change out some of the OEM switches - only the ones under the see-through polycarbonate Pixel Meow keycaps - for ones with a clear housing; I happened to have the switches on hand, but the stock switches wouldn't have looked bad, just (imho) not quite as good.

Instead of having full-time RGB, I opted for the setting where a section of keys briefly lights up as you type. The default color for that was white, but I downloaded and used the proprietary software to set the effect to a light pink.

With a firmware update (available on GravaStar's site) you can disable the LED logo screen's RGB, but the software does not appear to allow you to set a static color of your choice. By default, the LED logo acts as an indicator light, changing from RGB (default) to white (CapsLock). If you prefer, however, you can disable the indicator function with FN+CapsLock. I also couldn't see a software option to customize the RGB color for the outer frame, although the onboard settings offer decent flexibility. They very unfortunately don't have a very pale pink color option, despite the keyboard being pale pink.

Having said that, I don't actually have the border/ambient RGB on when using the keyboard in wireless mode - which is always, unless I need to charge the battery. Battery life feels infinite this way. Unlike many manufacturers, GravaStar didn't stint on the non-pro keyboard's batteries. The K1 Pro and K1 both use the same, huge, 8000mAh batteries. It's only the Lite version where you see compromises (plastic top case, half the battery capacity, no front/side ambient lighting).

GravaStar's support is also great, which I discovered when I had some questions about the keyboard. FYI, if you buy the keyboard on Amazon (US), GravaStar wants you to communicate through GravaStar US, which you can do here on Amazon. GravaStar's US support ALWAYS got back to me within 24 hours during our back-and-forth discussion, they were ALWAYS very customer service oriented, and were both kind and professional.

(Edited)

If you've had your eye on a GravaStar keyboard, seriously, just buy one. They're truly fantastic! I have since added a TickType DP104 full-size keyboard to my collection, which is solid aluminum and costs just under $200. It is INCREDIBLE and I am love with it....and my GravaStar keyboards truly are JUST as satisfying to type on. I equally love them, and am typing this on my blue GravaStar K1. I truly don't find one to be better than the other, overall, they're just DIFFERENT (particularly due to layout size, of course), which is amazing when the K1's are more affordable - MUCH more so if you catch them on sale.

Finally, I DO have two fairly nit-picky requests for GravaStar that will make this fabulous keyboard pretty much PERFECT:

1. Please stop putting the brand name on the front. And ESPECIALLY stop wrecking the white ones with dark print. At least the other colors have tone-on-tone, which makes it tolerable, but I haven't bought a white keyboard SOLELY due to the logo.

2. Stop teasing us with an LCD that isn't programmable. I want to have time/date. I want to upload GIFS. I want to AT LEAST be able to set a color or colors!

It’s a well-built keyboard with some excellent features and clever design choices. The cable is thick, long, and even has a nice touch — the SteelSeries logo on the USB plug. The RGB effects are top-notch, with smooth transitions both on keypress and when idle. I was genuinely excited about all of this... until I noticed what was missing. And for me, that’s a big deal.

Let’s break it down.😁

### What Makes It (Almost) 5 Stars – The Good:😃

- Excellent Media Controls: The volume wheel is fantastic: easy to reach, smooth to use, and includes a click-to-mute function. The menu button also works similarly to the playback controls found on many headsets with built-in microphones or hands-free kits. Super convenient.

- Onboard Controls – No Software Needed: You can manage brightness, RGB colors, effects, profiles, and more — all from the keyboard itself. No software required. Only macros can’t be directly viewed or edited in menu, which is a small detail worth noting.

- Smart OLED Display: It shows the status of Num Lock, Caps Lock, Scroll Lock, and whether the Windows key is disabled. Very handy (though there’s a small catch — more on that below).

- Customization & Visual Feedback: Besides full per-key RGB customization and reactive effects, pressing the “Fn” key (the SteelSeries logo key) lights up related function keys in red for quick reference. It’s super helpful… but again, not perfect (you can’t change the color — more on that too).

- Profile Memory Built-In: You can save up to 5 profiles directly on the keyboard and toggle them on/off without cycling through all of them. I personally use just two: one for gaming and one for productivity.

### The Not-So-Good – My Gripes😒:

- No Dedicated Context Menu Key: This is my biggest issue. A full-size keyboard should include the dedicated menu key (the "right-click menu" key). SteelSeries replaced it with their custom “Fn” key, which really disrupted my usual workflow. I ended up switching to Shift + F10 to keep things consistent across devices.

- Fn Key Can’t Be Reassigned: The SteelSeries logo key, which replaces the context menu key, is fixed — it can’t be remapped. Personally, I’d have preferred having the Windows key only on the left, and using the right one for Fn, keeping the menu key in its usual place.

- OLED Button Always Lit: The brightness of the button next to the OLED screen cannot be dimmed or turned off. If you’re working in a dark room or watching movies, this little light will keep shining at you — kind of annoying.

- OLED Icons Overlap Custom Logos: If you upload a custom image to the OLED screen, the status icons for Num Lock, Caps, etc. may overlap your logo. Not a dealbreaker, but it limits how creative you can get with personalization.

- No Visual Feedback When Windows Key Is Locked: Unlike other lock states (like Caps Lock), there’s no lighting change or visual indicator on the keyboard itself when the Windows key is disabled — just a small icon on the OLED. Feels inconsistent.

- Function Key Highlight Color Can’t Be Changed: When pressing “Fn,” the related keys light up red — but that red is not customizable. If your RGB theme is red, this effect becomes basically invisible.

- Slight Input Delay: There’s a small delay in key activation. I don’t notice it while typing or working, but for competitive gaming, it might matter. Rtings.com confirmed this in their testing too.

- Non-Replaceable Hybrid Switches This is the most serious issue. The switches aren’t standard and can’t be replaced by the user. If a key fails, you’re stuck with relying on warranty, support… or scavenging another board. Not great.

### Neutral Points – Might Be Good or Bad Depending on You🤷🏻‍♂️:

- Actuation Distance: I switched from a keyboard with ultra-light 0.8 mm actuation, and I kept typing extra characters. The Apex 5 feels much more precise and helped reduce typos — a big plus for me.

- Key Feel & Keycaps: The keycaps aren’t made from premium material, but they feel decent. Coming from linear switches, the tactile feel took a bit of getting used to — but I adjusted quickly.

- Magnetic Wrist Rest: I don’t use it much, but the magnets are strong and hold it firmly in place.

- Macro Labeling (M1, M2, etc.): Some keys are labeled as macro keys (M1, M2...), which can be confusing at first — but you’ll get used to it.

- Customization Without Software: You can change basic RGB effects and profiles directly from the keyboard. The software adds more depth, but it’s nice that you’re not forced to use it.

- USB Plug with Logo: A small but smart touch: the SteelSeries logo on the USB plug helps you spot which device you’re plugging in.

- No Physical Lock LEDs: The lock indicators (Num Lock, Caps, Scroll) have been moved to the OLED screen, and you can set those keys to change color when active. Some might miss the old-school LED lights, but I’m fine with it.

### Final Verdict 💸😇

 The SteelSeries Apex 5 is a well-built, visually polished keyboard with great RGB, useful media controls, and a solid set of features for gamers and professionals alike. Still, a few oversights — especially the missing context menu key and the non-replaceable switches — keep it from being a perfect 5-star device in my eyes.

If those flaws don’t bother you, then this keyboard is an easy recommendation. Just know what you're getting — and what you're not

I purchased it almost four years ago to replace the original Fitbit Versa. But then Google took over Fitbit, and I was looking for a reliable alternative to the Fitbit products. I tried a Samsung Galaxy watch 7 that lost steps by the thousands each day. I tried an Apple Smart Watch that sometimes had to be charged more than once EVERY DAY! I tried a Parsonver (less expensive) but even though it was advertised and labeled IP 68, (indicating that it would withstand submersion in water) I actually received an email from the company before the watch was even delivered advising me to be careful even showering or washing my hands with it on! SERIOUSLY???? And the step counts were not even close to correct! Then I tried an Amazfit BIP6 (also advertised as IP 68, but clearly IS NOT) and thought I had finally found what I was looking for, until it completely malfunctioned after only 3 weeks of use. So Amazon replaced it with ANOTHER BIP6, and that one lasted almost 5 months before it began to seriously malfunction and the touchscreen no longer worked. So my new search began and I decided to give Garmin a try as my walking and swimming buddies swear by their Garmins, and the results that they get with them compare favorably to my old Fitbit. I have now only had the Garmin Vivoactive 5 for about a month, but so far, it is AWESOME! It tracks extremely well with the Fitbit, and I have had no issues whatsoever with water infiltration. This proves that you don’t have to buy the most expensive models of ANY brand of fitness watch to find one that does what you need it to do. Most of them have more functions than you will ever need or use anyway. I bought separate, different color bands to customize it and love that you have a lot of choices for watch faces, so pick the one that works best for you! (Although - once again, Fitbit has a much better and more user friendly watch face selection portal!)

The one potential “glitch” I thought I had finally discovered with my Vivoactive 5, but which turned out not to be an issue, occurred when I was flying internationally. I was returning from Europe to the US on an evening flight where the time in the US was six hours earlier. So both my FITBIT and my Garmin thought that when enough flight time had elapsed, they went past midnight and started their metrics over as a new day - meaning steps completely zeroed out and started over. But not long after I landed at 7 pm US time, my Fitbit picked back up with the previous day’s step tally, but my Garmin still showed the reduced step count tallied as a “new day”. I was disappointed with this until I checked the metrics in the Garmin app and noted that the “two day tallies” indicated on the watch itself were actually (appropriately!) counted and displayed as a single day step counts in the app. So yes, I am sold on the Garmin. But I do still have to wonder why if FITBIT - even early versions - could have successfully addressed ALL of the issues I have found with so many competitor brands, why can’t all the others? Maybe I shouldn’t have been so wary of Google taking over Fitbit when I started investigating other Smart watches, but I learned a lot about different brands and their bogus IP 68 and 5 ATM ratings!

So to reiterate, Garmin is exactly what it says it is, and Fitbit is as well. Do your comparisons!

I do miss being able to use voice commands with my watch, but I could have gotten a more expensive Garmin if I really wanted that, and I don't think it's worth it for me.

The second thing I noticed: not having to charge your watch every day is a game changer. I couldn't charge it in the morning, because I like to start off my day with exercise and it doesn't charge fast enough to do it after a workout and before work. And if I charged it in the evening, I would often forget to put it on before bed and miss out on the sleep tracking. I took a multi day trip recently and I didn't once have to worry about charging my watch, which was a pleasant change.

Overall I think this watch is a great fit for a more casual user who isn't running marathons but wants to track fitness and sleep and get some extras like smartphone notifications and see the weather at a glance. I do like being able to track my sleep hours as well."}]

Read more"}, {"reviewer_name": "inayat2012 on youtube", "star_rating": 5.0, "review_title": "The fitbit killer", "review_description": "My wife and I have been fitbit fans since the Charge 2 (2016).  Before the google purchase, fitbit was a strong leader in lower cost fitness trackers.  It did concern us that our fitbits would die frequently (nearly each one we had died within a year from the Charge 2, 3, 4). So I looked around in late June and discovered the Fit 3.  So I bought one.  I am SO GLAD I did.  What do I need?  Step counter, heart rate, floors, distance, calories.  Oh, and the kicker for me was AIRPLANE MODE.  I study various energetic sciences including BioGeometry and the EMF coming from our devices is not benign.  I don't wear a tracker to sleep, don't want anything live, and keep my blue tooth turned off unless I am actively syncing.

This is what I see comparing Fit 3 to Fitbit Charge 6.   What the Fit 3 has as an advantage:  Larger screen, airplane mode, beautiful faces, much cleaner UI on the watch and in the android app(s) (I am using this with a Pixel 7 phone).  The ability to sync only turning on bluetooth.  A few years ago fitbit/google basically said we aren't syncing your fitbit unless you have both location/GPS and bluetooth turned on.  Sometimes you could get the fitbit to sync with location off but this was tricky/spotty.

What advantages did the Charge 6 have for me, personally.   None really.  It cost about 3x the amount for the Charge 6 compared to the Fit 3.  That's ridiculous.

In a head to head comparsion of measurements this is what I see.   Fitbit Charge is often slower to start your step counts and the Fit 3 is quicker on that.  So you steps counts are going to go up and perhaps the Fit 3 does count some arm motions as steps when it should not.  But the Fit 3 is still very close (within 1-3%) with the Charge 6.  The Fit 3 tends to undercount calories compared to the Charge 6, I can't tell which is more accurate.  On the Charge 6 bluetooth syncing was always a laborious pain taking sometimes minutes to get the past few days of data and often having to turn bluetooth off/on and/or restarts to get it to sync.  The Fit 3 is very fast *most* of the time.  I did have one instance where the Fit 3 was not syncing in the Health App and I had to open the Wearable app and trigger a sync from there, which worked.

The big thing is battery life.  I have automatic activity tracking turned on and except when syncing in the evening I keep it on airplane mode.  I charged it overnight last Thursday/Friday before I first put it on.  It's now Wednesday evening, nearing 6 complete days of use and my battery level is at 55%.  That frugal energy use is really good and is on par with the earlier monochrome fitbits.

I am very pleased with my Fit 3 purchase.  Back in the early to mid 2000's I was very excited about Timex was doing just in digital watches (Iron Man, etc).  The Fit 3 harkens back to those kind of days for me when you could get a very full functionality wrist device that looked good, worked great, and was a good deal.  This is definitely worth a close look if you don't need an higher priced fitness/communication device that is emitting EMFs into your pericardium meridian 24x7.  Well done.

Read more"}, {"reviewer_name": "Lauren C", "star_rating": 4.0, "review_title": "Nice fitness tracker", "review_description": "I've had a long line of Fit Bits and when I found out Samsung has a non-smart watch tracker, I decided to give it a chance. (I don't want to pay smart watch prices.)

It stayed English until I got a new phone and had to reset the tracker in order to pair it with the new phone. The charge on this item is supposed to last up to 13 days. I've had this device for 3 months, and I got 6 days out of each charge (7 if I let the device die) for the first 2 months or so. My Fit 3 charges from 20% to 70% in about 20 minutes and to 100% in about an hour. The trick is to get the charger properly seated, because the first couple of times, I don't think it was on correctly, as I got the main display, not the charging percentage display, and it took about 2 hours to reach 100%.

I wore the new Fit 3 side by side with my old Fitbit Charge 6 for 24+ hours to compare - 2 nights and one active day. The first night, the Fit 3 recorded 20 more minutes of sleep and the second night, the Fitbit recorded 20 more minutes. There are many more features that I don't use. I may in the future, but I'm happy with what I do use. I tried taking photos on my phone (also a Samsung) with my Fit 3 as a remote shutter button. I like that feature!

Text notifications come to my Fit 3, but not all of them. When I am using my phone, notifications do not go to the tracker (I have found that this is the default and I can change it if desired). Group texts never do (they will go to my car, so I don’t know why they won't go to my Fit 3), and random regular texts don't. I found in the Health app where I can pick and choose which apps will send notifications.

All told, I like this device. It’s not perfect, though. I miss the feature that Fitbit has that reminds me to move each hour. I like seeing the hearts light up throughout the day as I get closer to my goals. I also have active minutes and active calories burned as goals, but I don’t care as much about those.

I wear the watch while exercising - mainly yoga - and going about normal activity: no banging or brushing of the watch against any other items. BP and pulse seem to be good, pedometer is accurate. I don't wear at night so can't attest to accuracy of sleep functions [NOTE: I've replaced the watchband with no issues multiple times; new band in these photos].

I've been wearing this watch for 4 days. It charged quickly, and held the charge until now. The rose gold

is nice looking, with a pink strap. The watch face is black when asleep; you can awaken it by pressing the side button, or else change the setting through the app to awaken when you lift your arm.

To fully receive the benefit of the features of this smart watch, you need to download the Riversong app. A small booklet comes with the watch and provides the QR code and/or the web address. This booklet is basically a Quickstart guide. Since I have never had a smart watch before, I've been trying to figure out on my own how to use it and what I can actually do with it. For example, I know how to "wake up" the watch, but it's not self evident how to swipe to get to the different screens. Up? Down? Left? Right? Hit the button again? Who knows?

There are lots of options. Through the app you can set your preferred notifications, pair the watch with your phone, set a sedentary alert, set alarms. There's a heart monitor which provides your heart rate and blood pressure. I don't know if you can set it to give an alert if your readings are too high or too low. There's also a period tracker, but I don't know how it compares to other apps. I haven't tried the sport tracker yet.

reviews:
[{"reviewer_name": "frankbif", "star_rating": 5.0, "review_title": "Functional, Spiffy, Sleek, and Most Important.....USEFUL !!", "review_description": "This is my 1st purchase of a Garmin Smartwatch. I had several Fitbits in the past 10 years and I was pretty much satisfied with just using the basics of that simpler watch. Music, payments, advanced workouts, messages, all the rest – I never used my watch for those functions.

I was looking for a smartwatch to count my daily steps, track heartrate (see why below), quickie weather forecasts, a few stock quotes, oh yeah…and the time. That was pretty much the limits of my Fitbit usage. So having those plus a bunch of other simple apps or glances (Garmin’s terms for simple and oft-used apps), I was more than happy. The Garmin Venu 3S does all of this and more. If you want to do music, videos, payments, and lots of other features the Venu 3S can do those too, but that’s not my bag, as Austin Powers once said.

The glances features are pretty easy to navigate once you get comfortable with these app-like functions. The Body Battery function is interesting, combining data from several apps to determine how much energy your body has or needs. Sleep Score is also useful. I even found a nifty Sun & Moon app that gives me the time for sunrise/set and moonrise/set plus the Moon phase -- useful for my daily activities and those days and nights when I pursue my astronomy hobby.

I am especially pleased with the heart apps. I have several heart issues including HOCM (Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy) so being able to check my heart rate at rest and during rigorous walks is very important to me. The ECG and HRV Status apps are nice additional features to have (if you have an arrythmia check with your cardiologist/doctor before activating the ECG function). The Pulse Oximeter is also good to check upon during long walks or other strenuous activities.

Battery life consistently averaging 10 days is fantastic, especially compared to Apple smartwatches that need to be recharged in under 2 days. My Fitbits could last 5 days but that meant bringing a charger for most vacations or longer times away from home. The Venu 3S is able to last 10 days right on the dot, and that included during the setup run when the watch was being used a lot more and downloading updates, glances, apps, etc. A battery saver option with a “sleep” mode will help you survive until you can get back to your home and charger, preserving battery life if you’re using the watch but running low on power.

I got the Venu 3S instead of the brand new model 4S (which had just come out) because for someone not maxxing out on all the apps/glances/features, the 3S was more than enough for my needs. I didn’t see a revolutionary change from the Venu 3S to the 4/4s. If you are a person who lives more off their smartwatch than your smartphone, then perhaps the additional features and new OS (assuming no glitches) on the Garmin Venu 4 will be worth it. At an extra 20% in cost, make sure you need the latest features or it’s an unnecessary expenditure.

Net-Net: this is a really nifty smartwatch for the advanced or beginner smartwatch user. The interface is very nice…swiping is easy and seamless....button navigation also very simple...the watch face colors are bright and easy to see even in direct sunlight. The 41mm size is fine for me (I’m under 6 feet tall) and most people, but if you like having an oversized watch or are a bigger person with a bigger wrist, than the 45mm size of the Venu 3 might be better for you.

Very happy with my Garmin Venu 3S and if my prior experience with their GPS car navigation systems holds, I should have many years of trouble-free usage ahead of me.

If you want to record an activity or access one of your apps then you would press the top button. [{"reviewer_name": "Christopher Martin", "star_rating": 5.0, "review_title": "Ridge vs Anker 10,000mAh batteries", "review_description": "Tried both the Ridge 10,000mAh and the Anker 10,000mAh battery and the Anker charges MUCH faster and more than once! It doesn’t have the flexibility of the Ridge in terms of having different connectors (USB-C, Lightning, and Apple Watch), but the Ridge can barely charge an iPhone 17 Pro once! The magnetic connection on the Anker is fine but not as strong as it is on the Ridge. Both feel solid in terms of quality, with the Ridge feeling a bit more rugged and thick compared to the Anker’s slightly slimmer and sleeker form factor. It really comes down to your needs and if you need the ability to charge multiple devices and different connectors vs charging speed and sleekness."}, {"reviewer_name": "J.S.", "star_rating": 5.0, "review_title": "Immaculate 15W Qi2 speeds and a rock-solid magnetic lock—pricey but worth it in the end!", "review_description": "I picked up this Anker MagGo 10,000mAh Magnetic Power Bank to serve as my primary mobile charging solution for long days away from the workshop. High-end magnetic battery packs are always a significant investment, and this premium unit is definitely on the pricey side. However, after putting it through continuous real-world use, the exceptional hardware build quality and true ultra-fast charging performance make it completely worth it in the end.

Why this MagGo power bank is an exceptional wireless charger:

True 15W Ultra-Fast Qi2 Charging: Unlike older legacy magnetic battery packs that cap your wireless charging speeds at a sluggish, battery-heating 7.5W, this unit features official Qi2 certification. It pushes a full, unthrottled 15W of wireless power straight to your phone. It juices up modern devices from dead to 50% in a fraction of the time, easily matching the speed of a physical desktop wall brick.

Rock-Solid Magnetic Alignment: The internal magnet array is incredibly powerful. It snaps onto the back of a MagSafe-compatible phone case with a sharp, confidence-inspiring click. The alignment tracking is pristine; you can slide the phone into a tight pocket or use it aggressively while charging without the battery shifting, twisting, or losing its connection.

Sleek Ergonomic Slim Footprint: For a hefty 10,000mAh cell capacity, the physical ergonomics are brilliant. The edges are beautifully smoothed and tapered, allowing the battery pack to rest comfortably in your palm behind your phone without creating an exhausting, bulky brick feel during extended handheld use.

Premium ActiveShield 2.0 Thermal Safety: High-speed wireless charging naturally generates heat, which can degrade phone batteries. Anker's integrated temperature monitoring chipset operates flawlessly here. The housing gets warm to the touch under a full 15W dump, but it controls the thermal curve beautifully, preventing your device from overheating or throttling speeds.

Mobile Setup & Charging Tips:

Use a Qi2 or MagSafe Case: To guarantee the maximum magnetic holding force, ensure you are pairing this with a bare phone or a high-quality case equipped with a built-in magnetic ring. Trying to push a wireless charge through a thick, basic plastic case will severely weaken the magnets and cause energy loss.

Bi-Directional USB-C Port: The side Type-C port works both ways. Beyond rapid self-recharging, you can plug a physical cable into it to charge a secondary device (like a tablet or wireless headphones) simultaneously while your phone charges wirelessly on the pad face.

The final verdict:Anker has engineered a flawless, studio-grade portable power station that entirely removes the slow-charging frustrations of older wireless packs. The materials feel incredibly robust, the digital battery percentage indicator is crisp and clear, and the 15W throughput is legendary. If you are tired of cheap, sluggish battery packs cooking your phone, this premium Qi2 unit is an absolute home run upgrade.

Bigger than the pictures suggest but still portable."}, {"reviewer_name": "Michael", "star_rating": 4.0, "review_title": "Reasonable effective capacity vs claimed capacity", "review_description": "Purchased this power bank (INIU B1-B5 20000mAh) due to seeing YouTube review of several PBs where reviewer took apart several PBs and showed that the batteries used in the PBs were actually rated far below the claimed capacities. INIU was one of few brands whose battery (in this case 20000mAh) label actually matched the advertised capacity. IOW, some brands that advertised 20000mAh capacity actually had batteries in them that were listed at 10000mAh etc.

I used an old iPhone 7plus (with a 2900mAh battery) to charge from 50% back to 100% (or 1450mAh). The INIU B1-B5 went from 100% down to 86% (test was done three times with same results). Due to voltage conversion from the 3.7v battery to 5v USB output, the effective total capacity of the PB should be around (3.7/5)*20000 or 14800mAh. Since 14% of the PB was used, this amounts to 2072mAh. Since 2072 mAh of output from the PB was used to effectively charge 1450mAh of the phone battery, this amounts to a 70% charging efficiency. This means that I would get around 3.57 charges of my old iPhone 7plus out of this 20000mAh battery power bank.

IIRC, I read somewhere that the expected efficiency of power banks should average around 80-85% due to conversion losses. At 70% loss, this power bank does not seem to be every efficient (although in my test, this may be due in part to the fact that the phone used is an old one).

The positives: This power bank did charge my phone from 50% to 100 % in 1hr 57min which is pretty good given the iPhone 7plus is not fast charge (PD) capable. In my short time with the INIU, it seems to hold a charge well, did not heat up and did not heat up the phone while charging. It was also consistent in the charge times.

The neutrals: While the thickness and weight of the unit does not lend itself to carry in a pocket while charging your phone (see specs on Amazon page), it is compact enough to easily carry in your carry on luggage as at a rated 74Wh it is well below the 100Wh limit imposed by the FAA and airlines. While it did underperform regarding capacity vs what it is advertised to be able to do, it was not as bad as some of the other power banks I tested, and came the closest to the advertised capacity as compared to some of the others I tested.

The negatives: All power banks seem to use misleading specs in their advertising. Just because the power bank has a “20000mah” battery, does not mean that it will charge a device with, say a 4000mAh battery 5 times. Far from this due to various conversion losses etc. Also, I assume that these conversion losses can vary quite a bit between various power banks. While this power bank seems to not be very efficient, it met my needs (especially for the price).

Unknowns: I have only just gotten this power bank and have only used it 4 times to charge my phone from 50% back to 100%. I anticipate using it primarily for travel. 1. This product does have different color lights . 2. You can turn the color cycling off so that it stays on whatever color you desire. 3. You are able to adjust the brightness, there are three levels

The thing to keep in mind is you navigate this one button device with the timing of your button presses. A long 3 second tap will turn it on and off. The default when you turn it on is the white color. The white is not too cool, nor too warm. You can adjust the brightness and at the highest level it is plenty bright if you need to find something in the room. I don’t think it will adequately light a large dark room on its own. But you can read using this light if you are within a few feet of the lamp (for most people).

. If you want to change to the color setting, then a quick one second tap after the device is turned on. At this point, you will be on the color cycling mode. if you do nothing, the device will cycle through various shades of green, blue, red, yellow, etc. For example, you will see a turquoise blue, a cornflower blue, a hot pink, a pale green, etc. If you want to select a particular color, wait until it cycles to the color you like, and use a one second tap to select. This will pause it on the color that was lit when you tapped the button.

If you want to turn the device off, just press the button for three seconds. Let me lead with the good, because there is plenty of it.

The light itself is genuinely nice. Plenty of brightness for working, reading, or close-up tasks, and the color temperature options give you warm yellow, neutral white, and a cooler white-blue depending on what you are doing. Eleven brightness levels is more granularity than I expected. The arm extends and folds well, and the head pivots to put light right where you want it. It runs on USB, the wall adapter is included, and the wattage is low enough that you can power it from a laptop port if that is convenient. The clamp mount is solid and holds tight once you have it in place.

A note on installation. The clamp wants a specific amount of mounting surface, and my location had less than the lamp wanted in one direction. I pulled out a Dremel and shaved a small relief into the underside so the clamp could sit properly. Not a complaint, just a heads up if your desk has a thick lip, a beveled edge, or a rounded corner where you want this to live.

Now, the big thing.

This lamp does not default to on when power is restored. If you turn it off and walk away, fine. If your power blips, or if you have it on a smart switch that cuts power, the lamp comes back off. To turn it back on you have to walk over to the lamp and press the little button on the inline cord controller, which sits close to the base of the arm and is not always easy to reach.

This matters because the listing advertises a memory function, and modern buyers, especially anyone with a smart home setup, are going to read that and assume something it does not actually mean. Here is what is happening. The memory function does work, in a narrow sense. When you press the on button, the lamp comes back at whatever brightness and color mode you used last. It does not have to be reset every time. That is real and it is useful.

What the memory function does not do is preserve the on/off state across a power cut. The reason is that this is a soft-touch push button rather than a mechanical switch. The lamp's electronics have to be powered to know they are on, and when power is removed and restored the default state is off. A traditional mechanical switch physically holds the circuit closed and is why your bedroom lamp comes back on when the power flickers. This one does not, by design.

If you live in a fully manual lighting world, this is a non-issue. You will press the button and life goes on. If you have your office lights on a smart switch, or you have ever said the words "Google (or Alexa), turn on the lights," this is going to be an ongoing minor annoyance. If you are mounting this on the back edge of a desk that sits against a wall, on the lip of a hutch, on top of a shelving unit, or inside a cubicle, you are going to discover that the elbow needs room to bow outward behind the lamp. There is also a 45 minute auto-off timer button on the controller. Apparently aimed at bedtime reading. I have not used it but it is there if you want it.

Four stars. The light is good and the build is good. The memory function exists but means something different than a smart home buyer will assume, and the mounting flexibility has limits that the listing does not show. If you can live with those, this is a nice lamp at a fair price. If you were hoping to drop it into an automated lighting routine, you are going to want to know about the default-off behavior before you order.

[{"reviewer_name": "Shawn R.", "star_rating": 5.0, "review_title": "A really great air purifier that has many key improvements/advantages over its competitors", "review_description": "I got this air purifier for a relative that has COPD. They already had an Alen T100 that they were pleased with. But, as is common in multiple industries where a core product requires a consumable, it's often not the condition of the core product but the availability of the required consumable that dictates when a product has to be replaced. While I've been able to find enough replacement air filters for that one air purifier, when the need arose for a 2nd air purifier for a second section of the house, instead of just getting a newer Alen, I opted to start the research process all over again and, this time, the clear winner was Coway And, as well as the Alen has done over the years, it didn't take long to see how much better the Coway model was by comparison. A first major difference is in the design and aesthetics. With several color variants and another model with a more classic look, it doesn't visually stand out as much as a typical tower air purifier does. It's more stylish and "elegant". Second, there are actual very practical functional reasons for those aesthetics. Instead of blowing air on people horizontally, it blows the air straight up so that nobody feels the air blowing. It's also significantly quieter so even set on medium speed it's quieter than the Alen at low speed. That's impressive given that this model is designed to handle a space 3X as much as the Alen was. But, it's due to the design of having the air come in from the sides and then exit out the top. It just provides a much more natural method of air circulation. And, also means it can be tucked along a wall and out of the way ... with the cord blocked from view if located directly at the power outlet. Another great feature that the Coway has that I haven't seen before is that you have 4 stage filtration .... with the initial pre-screen stage being a built-in filter that can be washed ... followed by the 1st charcoal filter to catch large objects like hair .... followed by a 2nd filter that have 4 replacement options and therefore can be customized based on what types of odors or particles a person needs filtered out ... and finally the HEPA filter that catches the smallest particles that make it past the other three. Not only is this like a coin-sorter process of filtering out different things at different people ... but this is why, unlike a lot of air purifiers, the main filters can last 1 year instead of just 6 months. The built-in filter is recommended to be cleaned once a month. The charcoal filter 6 months. The "environmental/smell" filter being replaced once a year. And, the HEPA filter being able to last even longer depending on environment. Where it actually gets better at filtering over time ... but then the tradeoff is air flow reduction. That's why the official recommendation is still once a year. And, best of all, the NYT wirecutter review I'd found says Coway has made continual improvements over the years to this product, which really shows. Many manufacturer's just seem intent on constantly reinventing the wheel and it seems Coway was instead focusing on perfecting what it already had. Very pleased with the results and the good deal we'd gotten on it. While we hope the Alen continues to do well for several more years, at least it's nice knowing that we already know what to replace it with whenever it become necessary.

3) Recipes for beef stews might limit the volume of potatoes, carrots, and onions to fit in the pot. An 8-quart pot allows me to use a larger cut of beef, and add more potatoes without jeopardizing the PC's ability to come up to pressure.

4) PC recipes that take longer than an hour test my patience for hanging around. I like to "set it and forget it" for a while.

5) Ribs. Ribs take up a lot of space, and most people don't limit themselves to a proper "single" portion. Set dry-rubbed ribs on a trivet in the PC and let the water's steam produce moist ribs. No BBQ sauce is needed!

I still use my smaller stovetop PCs for:

1) 3-qt is perfect size for rice. I prefer PC rice to rice cooker rice - less scorching. I freeze extra cooked rice.

2) 2-qt is perfect for simple dinner for 2 - and fast - it takes little time to come up to pressure or for natural release.

3) 5-qt braiser holds a full-size round cooling rack, allowing me to steam 4-5 chicken breasts or quickly steam asparagus.

4) I use the 5-qt braiser when I need a truly "quick release" to add foods in stages. With a stovetop PC, you take the PC to the sink and run cold water on the lid to reduce the pressure quickly. You can't do that with an electric cooker.

So, how about the 8-quart Instant Pot?

1) The inner pot is high quality. Soaking solves a lot of cleaning problems in stainless steel.

2) The silicone gasket fits very snugly. In fact, after I did my preliminary sudsy wash, it seemed like torture to get the gasket to fit correctly. I thought I had fit it correctly... until I tried to do the Water Test and I was unable to lock the lid in position. Thank goodness some kind souls on the Instant Pot Community page on Facebook helped me identify the problem. (When you get your 8-qt pot, observe carefully how the gasket fits before disassembling for washing.) Today,when I reassembled my IP, I patiently positioned the ring in one spot and patiently coaxed it into place, so apparently this old dog could still learn a new trick. (It is important that the gasket and the lid both be completely dry!)

3) The 8-qt. machine is BIG, and TALL. My kitchen counters are the high standard height, and it seemed awkward to me to try to saute in the Instant Pot. (One person suggested strongly that I use a step ladder - obviously no senior should try sauteing from a ladder.) With my beef stew recipe, I had planned to saute mushrooms and onions on the stove anyway (both emit a LOT of liquid, plus there is more "umami" when prepared this way) and add them to the stew at the end. So I sauteed the beef in the same 6 3/4 qt Le Creuset pot I was going to use for the mushrooms (I don't flip as much food out of that pot as when I use a normal saute pan). My method worked fine for me. If you dread cleaning an extra pot/pan, then you might choose to do everything in the Instant Pot - your choice. Today I reflected that I might use a table at the lower standard counter height, which would make it easier for me to saute in the Instant Pot itself, as long as the cord reached. (I loved the oval pot of the Cooks Essential PC - it was so easy to saute in it!)

4) The IP came up to pressure and down from pressure faster than the Cooks Essential PC. For a "quick" release, you don't have to wait as long before letting some steam out. And once the steam lever was released, the pressure came down very fast - that was a huge improvement over the Cook's Essential.

5) You can choose different settings for "Saute": great when you want a simmer and not a rapid boil!

6) There was plenty of extra room in the pot for the additional potatoes and carrots DH wants in the next batch.

7) Our beef stew was delightful, just as mouth-watering as doing the whole nine yards of Julia Child's Boeuf Bourguignon.

I am looking forward to trying many more recipes in this versatile cooker.

p.s. The packaging impressed me a lot! There was a reinforced plastic strap around the Instant Pot shipping box that made it easy to remove from the slightly larger Amazon shipping box. Inside the Instant Pot shipping box was the product box with all the graphics as you might see on a store shelf. The product box also had a plastic strap to coax the product box out of the Instant Pot shipping box. The product box had styrofoam reinforcement of the product at top and bottom. **Why I went with the Instant Pot (IP) duo60 Plus -

Three new preset buttons - cake, egg, sterilize. It also had the yogurt function which other IP do, but not some of the other makes.

Large LCD Screen with Digital Display

Mute button for those beeps in the night when cooking yogurt etc.

Plus / Minus button for both time and pressure

Delay start of 24 hours and keep warm for 10 hours.

Lid rest (right or left side)

**Why I went with IP vs PPCXL -

Food Grade 304 (15/8) stainless steel pot vs stainless steel with teflon coating. I felt I could scrub and treat the pot however I wanted and not worry about scratching and what utensils to not use. Yes, you can buy a replacement inner pot for a Teflon pot, but after I spend $100+ I really don't think I should have to buy a replacement inner pot.
